meta.description: The Bible never says money is the root of all evil. 1 Timothy 6:10 says the LOVE of money is—a one-phrase drop that flips the meaning. The real text, verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Money is the root of all evil'?
meta.ogDescription: 1 Timothy 6:10 condemns the LOVE of money, not money. The popular quote drops three words and reverses the meaning. Greek and KJV text, verified.

answer.label: Not in the Bible as worded — a misquote of 1 Timothy 6:10
answer.authorDates: Epistle traditionally ascribed to Paul the Apostle · 1st century AD
answer.sourceLine: The verse this comes from does not say money is the root of all evil. In the King James Version, 1 Timothy 6:10 reads “For the love of money is the root of all evil” — the Greek is philargyria (φιλαργυρια), ‘love of money.’ Dropping those three words turns a warning about greed into a condemnation of money itself, which the passage never makes.

source.heading: The verse behind the misquote

source.excerpt: For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
trail: The Koine Greek reads hē philargyria (φιλαργυρια), literally ‘the love of money’ — not money — as shown in the interlinear Greek and KJV at BibleHub.
Fact-checkers note the verse “is often misquoted as saying, ‘Money is the root of all evil’” — per GotQuestions.org.
The misquote substitutes ‘money’ for ‘love of money’ — but, as BibleStudyTools notes, “only the love of money is evil, not money itself.”
source.excerptNote: King James Version (1611). Modern translations render it “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (e.g. NIV, ESV) — a further softening of the sweeping ‘the root of all evil.’

source.rightsNote: The popular saying is a folk paraphrase, not a verbatim quotation, so it has no single copyright holder. The verse it derives from — 1 Timothy 6:10 in the King James Version (first published 1611) and its Koine Greek original — is long in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Paul the Apostle
author.heading: Whose warning was actually misquoted
author.metaLine: 1st century AD · Apostle & letter-writer of the early Church
author.bio: The First Epistle to Timothy, from which this line comes, is traditionally ascribed to Paul the Apostle, though many modern scholars regard the Pastoral Epistles as written later in his name. Whoever the author, the Greek text is unambiguous: it warns against philargyria, the love of money — the appetite for wealth, not wealth itself. The popular saying that drops those words says something the letter never did.

copyAttribution: Misquote of the Bible, 1 Timothy 6:10. The verse (KJV) says "the love of money is the root of all evil" — not money itself.

misattribution.heading: What the Bible actually says
misattribution.intro: “Money is the root of all evil” is one of the most common misquotations of Scripture. The line people cite is a shortened, meaning-altered version of a single verse.

items.why: The verse condemns the love of money, not money. KJV: “For the love of money is the root of all evil.” The Greek philargyria (φιλαργυρια) means ‘love of money’ — confirmed in the interlinear Greek.
Dropping ‘the love of’ blames money itself; as BibleStudyTools notes, “only the love of money is evil, not money itself.” Many translations soften it further to ‘a root of all kinds of evil.’

misattribution.truthLine: The Bible never says money is the root of all evil; it says the love of money is — a warning about greed, not wealth (GotQuestions).

context.heading: Why the missing words matter
lead: The three dropped words — ‘the love of’ — carry the entire ethical point. The verse is not an indictment of commerce, wealth, or coins; it is a warning about desire: the craving for money that, the letter says, leads some to “wander from the faith.” The misquote flattens a caution about the human heart into a slogan against money as such.
detailsBody: The KJV’s ‘the root of all evil’ itself sharpens the Greek, where the definite article is absent before the predicate. Modern translations such as the NIV and ESV render it ‘a root of all kinds of evil,’ presenting greed as one source of many troubles rather than the single origin of everything wrong — a reading closer to the Greek.
context.pull: It is not money, but the love of money, that the verse condemns.
